chapter: Hampton, Andy Kirk and Charlie Barnet
title: Hearing Charlie Parker on the radio and at the Savoy
summary: A radio broadcast of Jay McShann with Bird playing 'Cherokee' stuns McGhee and friends; they go to the Savoy to hear him, and later he hangs out with Bird and Dizzy in Philadelphia.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: The first time you heard Bird was when? When you were
Yeah.
And you all heard the radio program...
Yeah.
...and went up to the Savoy.
Yeah.
Which is a famous story.

Yeah, it was. I mean, to hear a guy like that out of nowhere, click, you turn on the radio and Bird comes jumping through the air. What the fuck is this? Who is that? What is that? And what the fuck is he playing? Oh, that was something else, man. Oh boy, that was really something else. I can't get over how amazing that really was, man. I didn't really believe it was... I said, "There's something wrong with the radio, man. This shit ain't comin' out right." But man, he was... Shit, he was play-ay-in', man!
But being an arranger and having learned the changes and stuff...
That's what I'm talking about, yeah.
...you could hear that.
I could hear what he was doing, and I knew what he was doing was right, and I was saying, "Damn, man! Who is that?" And we all, man... Everybody...we was all

laughing and talking, and all of a sudden it got quiet, nobody said a word, man, until after Bird got through playing. And the guy said, "Well, that's Jay McShann, comin' to the Savoy Ballroom" and I said "Oh boy, I know where I'm going tonight." So everybody said the same thing, said, "Yeah, I'm going with you."

So we went up to the Savoy, and I asked Jay... I said, "Jay, who was that saxophone player you had playing today?" So he told me. He said, "Oh, that's that guy sitting right over there." I said, "What's his name?" He said, "Oh, that's Charlie Parker." I said, "Yeah, that's the guy that played 'Cherokee' today on the radio?" He said, "Yeah." I said, "Well, bring him around front; I want to hear him." He says, "Okay, wait til I play a couple of tunes, then I'll bring him down front." And he brought him down, and Bird came down there -- and everybody stood there with their mouth wide open. We couldn't believe this motherfucker was playing that much horn. Pshew-whee!

And from then on, man, every time there was an opportunity for me to be with Bird... Like, I was with Barnet over in Philadelphia, we were playing three weeks at a ballroom over there, and he was with Earl Hines...
Playing tenor.
Yeah. And we all stayed at the Showboat

Hotel. After I'd get off of work, I'd go by, and they'd be there when I got there, because they played in a theatre and we played a ballroom. So I'd go in, and Dizzy and Bird were there, and Diz and I got to be, you know, tight, and I saw what he was doing and what he was playing -- and I guess that's where it rubbed off on me. Because I could do the same thing he was doing, and I had the range, so I didn't have to worry about going upstairs -- whenever he went upstairs, I could go upstairs, too. In fact, I used to have to hit his G's for him. He played "Salt Peanuts" [SINGS 8 BARS], at the end, after he'd get through playing his run and playing his solo, and Billy would give a chord for the downbeat, I had to hit the high G right there, because Dizzy couldn't make it...
Oh, this was in Eckstine's band.
Yeah, in Eckstine's band.
This was later.
Oh, this was much later on, yeah. I'll tell you about that, too, when we get to it.
All right, when we get to that. And we can double back, you know, and get into specifics. But I think maybe we should just go ahead with your career first.
Yeah, okay.
